questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.problem: Use the first three terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of $\sqrt{10}.$ Give your answer to $5$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{1/2} \\ f(9) & =3 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =\frac{1}{6} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(9) & =-\frac{1}{108}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =3+\frac{1}{6}(x-9)+\frac{1}{2!}(-\frac{1}{108})(x-9)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =3+\frac{1}{6}(x-9)-\frac{1}{216}(x-9)^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=10$ into the above to approximate $\sqrt{10}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10} & ≈3+\frac{1}{6}(10-9)-\frac{1}{216}(10-9)^{2} \\  & =3+\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{216} \\  & =3.162\,04,\end{aligned}
$$

to five decimal places.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.problem: Find the first three non-zero terms in the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ centered about the point $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $a=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{(5)}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{(5)}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0+(-1)(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{0}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2} \\  & +\frac{1}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{0}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}+\frac{(-1)}{5!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯ \\  & =-(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{6}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}-\frac{1}{120}{(x-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{5}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.problem: Find the first three non-zero terms in the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)$ about the point $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)$ and $a=2.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ f(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡6 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(2) & =-\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡6+(\frac{1}{2})(x-2)+\frac{1}{2!}(-\frac{1}{4})(x-2)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡6+\frac{1}{2}(x-2)-\frac{1}{8}(x-2)^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ and $a=\frac{3\pi }{4}.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\ f\,(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =cot\,(\frac{3\pi }{4})=-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-{csc}^{2}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}\,(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =-{csc}^{2}\,(\frac{3\pi }{4})=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =-1+(-2)(x-\frac{3\pi }{4})+⋯ \\  & =-1-2(x-\frac{3\pi }{4})+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}+0.2$ into the above to approximate $cot\,(\frac{3\pi }{4}+0.2).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}cot\,(\frac{3\pi }{4}+0.2) & ≈-1-2(\frac{3\pi }{4}+0.2-\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =-1-2(0.2) \\  & =-1-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
